name: Image Background Edge Checker
description: Preview a PNG with transparency over solid colors and a checkerboard to catch halos, fringe and messy cut-out edges before you submit or publish it.
body:
🖼️

Drop a PNG with transparency here or click to browse

Processed locally — nothing is uploaded

No transparency detected — this checker is designed for images with alpha channels. Try a PNG with transparent areas.

Preview

—Dimensions
—Color mode
—Transparency

Edge check tips

  • Zoom to 200–400% and look along the edges for a light or dark outline (halo).
  • Switch between red, green and blue — a colored fringe usually shows leftover background.
  • Check hair, fur and complex edges — they hide fringe the most.
howto: Upload a PNG (or WebP) with transparency using the dropzone.
Switch between the checkerboard and solid color backgrounds to inspect the edges.
Use the zoom slider to inspect edges up close.
Watch for halos, colored fringes or leftover background chunks along the outline.
Fix the cut-out in your editor, re-upload and re-check before submitting.
features: Checkerboard plus white, black, red, green and blue backgrounds
Zoom slider for close edge inspection
Color mode and transparency stats for your image
Warns you when an image has no transparency

faq.q: What is a halo in a PNG?
faq.a: A halo is a light or dark outline around the subject that remains after a rough background removal. It is the most common reason a cut-out looks unprofessional and a frequent cause of stock rejections.

faq.q: Why do colored backgrounds help catch bad edges?
faq.a: White and black can hide thin halos. Strong red, green or blue backgrounds make even a faint fringe visible, because leftover background pixels are almost never the same color as the backdrop.

faq.q: Does this tool fix my image edges?
faq.a: No. It is a checker, not an editor. It shows you the problem so you can fix it in your image editor, then re-check here.

faq.q: What is the best background for the final export?
faq.a: For stock submissions, export on a transparent background with a checkerboard preview so reviewers can see the true edges. The checkerboard pattern is the industry standard for judging cut-outs.
